country.name: Greece
country.tagline: Four thousand years of wine on islands and mountains, now poured as some of the most electric whites and age-worthy reds of the Mediterranean.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (vineyard area includes table grapes and currants; 2025 output recovered from 1.4 mhl in both 2023 and 2024, still below Greece's historical 2 to 4 mhl range)

country.overview:
Greece is where European wine culture learned to talk about itself. The Mycenaeans wrote the word for wine in Linear B, Homer gave the sea its colour from it, and the classical symposium turned a jug of watered wine into the setting for philosophy. Chian and Thasian wines travelled the Mediterranean in stamped amphorae, and the island of Thasos passed some of the first known laws regulating the wine trade. When modern wine lovers argue about origin, place and authenticity, they are continuing a conversation that started here.

Then came a long interruption. Byzantine Monemvasia shipped sweet Malmsey to all of Europe through Venetian hands, but four centuries of Ottoman rule taxed and hemmed in viticulture, and the young Greek state of the nineteenth century grew currants and bulk wine rather than fine bottles. Retsina, resinated white wine with roots in antiquity, became the national carafe. Phylloxera arrived late, in Macedonia from 1898, and ravaged the mainland while sparing the volcanic and limestone islands where vines still grow on their own roots.

The modern story begins in 1971 with the first appellation law and accelerates after Greece joined the European Community in 1981, when its appellations entered the EU register. A generation of producers trained in Bordeaux, Burgundy and Dijon came home in the 1980s and 1990s: Evangelos Gerovassiliou, Yiannis Boutaris, the Tsantalis family, Leon Karatsalos and Yiannis Paraskevopoulos of Gaia, George Skouras, Yiannis Tselepos. Some planted Cabernet and Chardonnay; the more lasting achievement was rediscovering what Greece already had. Gerovassiliou saved Malagousia from near extinction, the Zafeirakis family put Limniona on labels, and Santorini's growers turned Assyrtiko into the Mediterranean's answer to Chablis.

That native palette is the reason to care. Greece counts somewhere around 300 indigenous varieties, and the important ones are genuinely distinct: Assyrtiko holds bone-dry acidity in a hot island summer; Xinomavro, the 'acid-black' grape of Macedonia, gives pale, tannic reds that smell of tomato leaf, olive and dried roses and age like Nebbiolo; Agiorgitiko, from Nemea, is soft, plummy and generous; Moschofilero from the high Mantinia plateau is a pink-skinned aromatic white of rose petal and citrus. Add Malagousia, Roditis, Savatiano, Vidiano, Robola, Limnio, Liatiko, Mavrodaphne and the Muscats of Samos, Patras and Limnos and you have one of the richest ampelographic collections in Europe.

Geography explains the range. Greece is four-fifths mountains, and altitude rather than latitude sets the style: Amyndeon in the far north-west grows grapes at 600 to 750 metres beside four lakes and makes sparkling wine, while Santorini's vines crouch in wind-woven baskets on bare pumice at sea level. The Ionian and Aegean seas temper the heat, the meltemi wind dries the islands, and limestone, schist, volcanic ash and red clay change every few kilometres. Thirty-three Protected Designations of Origin (PDOs) cover the classic places, from Naoussa and Nemea to the four Malvasia appellations created in 2011 to revive the medieval sweet wine trade, and more than a hundred Protected Geographical Indications (PGIs) give room to blends and international grapes.

The recent news is climatic. The 2023 and 2024 harvests each fell to about 1.4 million hectolitres, among the smallest in modern records, after heatwaves, drought and wildfires; Santorini's 2024 crop was tiny even by its own miserly standards, and prices for island Assyrtiko have climbed accordingly. The OIV puts the 2025 harvest at 1.6 million hectolitres, a partial recovery that still leaves Greece well below its historical two to four million. The upside is a country that already farms some of the most heat-resilient grapes in Europe, and a wave of growers working old vines on their own roots, high-altitude sites and forgotten varieties. For a wine nerd, Greece is a place where the most ancient story and the newest bottle are often the same thing.

history.title: Pressed grapes at Dikili Tash
history.text: Charred grape pips and pressed skins in a Late Neolithic house at Dikili Tash, near Philippi in eastern Macedonia, are among the earliest evidence of grape pressing in the Aegean, more than a thousand years before the palaces of Crete.

history.title: Minoan presses and the buried town of Akrotiri
history.text: The Minoan villa at Vathypetro above Archanes kept a stone wine press and storage jars, and on Thera the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri was sealed with its jars and vessels under volcanic ash by the great eruption. The same pumice now feeds Santorini's ungrafted Assyrtiko.

history.title: Wine in Linear B
history.text: Mycenaean clay tablets from the Palace of Nestor at Pylos and from Knossos use an ideogram for wine and record vineyards, wine rations and a palace wine magazine with dozens of storage jars: the first written Greek wine administration.

history.title: Thasos regulates the wine trade
history.text: Inscriptions from Thasos set rules on when and how Thasian wine could be sold and shipped, and its stamped amphorae turn up across the Black Sea and the Aegean. It is one of the earliest legal frameworks for a named wine.

history.title: Chian wine, the classical grand cru
history.text: Wine from the Ariousian hills of Chios was the luxury bottle of the classical world, shipped in distinctive amphorae with a swollen neck and stamped with a sphinx. Athenian comedy and Roman writers treated it as the benchmark.

history.title: Malmsey sails from Monemvasia
history.text: From the fortified rock of Monemvasia, Venetian merchants shipped a sweet wine that Europe called Malvasia, Malvoisie or Malmsey. The name outlived the trade and attached itself to grapes from Madeira to the Lipari islands.

history.title: Gustav Clauss builds Achaia Clauss
history.text: A Bavarian merchant founded a castle-like winery in the hills above Patras and made a fortified red from Mavrodaphne that became Greece's best-known export wine of the nineteenth century.

history.title: Phylloxera reaches Macedonia
history.text: The louse arrived late, devastating the northern mainland vineyards in the early twentieth century, while Santorini's ash, Kefalonia's limestone scree and other islands stayed free of it, which is why ungrafted, centuries-old root systems survive there.

history.title: The first appellation law
history.text: Greece created its system of quality appellations, with Nemea and Naoussa among the first zones delimited. After accession to the European Community in 1981 the appellations entered the EU register.

history.title: Domaine Carras and the birth of modern Greek wine
history.text: John Carras planted a modern estate on the slopes of Mount Meliton in Sithonia with advice from Émile Peynaud; the Slopes of Meliton appellation followed in 1982. The estate also helped rescue Malagousia, which Evangelos Gerovassiliou, its winemaker, later made famous at Epanomi.

history.title: The Malvasia appellations return
history.text: Four PDOs were registered for sweet wines from sun-dried grapes in the medieval Malvasia tradition: Monemvasia-Malvasia, Malvasia Paros, Malvasia Sitia and Malvasia Chandakas-Candia.

history.title: Heat, drought and two tiny harvests
history.text: Greece produced about 1.4 million hectolitres in both 2023 and 2024, its smallest crops in modern records, before a partial recovery to 1.6 million in 2025 according to the OIV.

country.classification:
Greek wine labels follow the EU pyramid. At the top sit the 33 PDOs (ΠΟΠ, Prostatevomeni Onomasia Proelefsis), most registered in 1981 when Greece joined the European Community; their rules fix varieties, yields and styles, and several are tied to a single grape (Naoussa to Xinomavro, Nemea to Agiorgitiko, Mantinia to Moschofilero, Patra to Roditis). Below them more than a hundred PGIs (ΠΓΕ) range from regional names such as Macedonia or Peloponnese to small zones such as Florina, Drama or Plagies Ampelou on Samos, and allow international varieties and blends. Varietal wines without geographical indication and plain wine sit at the bottom.

Three things trip up newcomers. First, many of the best bottles are PGIs, because estates blend native and international grapes or work outside a PDO's grape rules. Second, Greece keeps traditional terms: Retsina is protected as a 'traditional appellation' for resinated wine, Verdea for the oxidative whites of Zakynthos, and Vinsanto belongs to Santorini alone. Third, ageing words differ by category: Reserve and Grand Reserve are reserved for PDO wines, while Cava is used for aged PGI and table wines. Ktima means estate, Monastiri a monastery, Archontiko a manor.
country.climate_soils:
A Mediterranean climate is bent out of shape by mountains and seas. Most vineyards sit between sea level and 1,000 metres, and altitude decides ripeness: Amyndeon (570 to 750 m) and Mantinia (around 650 m) are cool enough for sparkling wine, while the Peloponnese coast and Crete are hot and dry. The northern meltemi blows across the Aegean all summer, cooling the islands and keeping disease pressure low, but it also forces growers into low bush vines and, on Santorini, into woven baskets.

Soils are a mosaic. Santorini has volcanic ash and pumice with almost no clay, which is why phylloxera never took hold; Kefalonia's Robola grows in limestone scree on Mount Ainos; Naoussa mixes marl, clay and limestone with sandy patches; Nemea runs from red clay on the valley floor to limestone and stony soils at 600 to 850 metres; Crete offers calcareous marls and clay. Water stress is the defining modern problem, and drought farming of old, low-yielding bush vines is both a tradition and a climate strategy.

grapes.name: Assyrtiko
grapes.note: Santorini's flagship white, now planted all over Greece and abroad; holds piercing acidity and saline, smoky intensity even in heat. The basis of dry Santorini, Nykteri and Vinsanto.

grapes.name: Xinomavro
grapes.note: The great red of Macedonia (Naoussa, Amyndeon, Goumenissa, Rapsani): pale, tannic and acidic, with tomato, olive and dried-rose aromas; long-lived and often compared with Nebbiolo.

grapes.name: Agiorgitiko
grapes.note: Nemea's red: soft tannins, plum and cherry fruit, versatile from rosé to oak-aged reserves and sweet styles.

grapes.name: Moschofilero
grapes.note: Pink-skinned aromatic white from the Mantinia plateau: rose, citrus and spice with crisp acidity; also made as sparkling and rosé.

grapes.name: Malagousia
grapes.note: Aromatic white rescued from near extinction in the 1970s and popularised by Gerovassiliou at Epanomi: peach, jasmine and herbs.

grapes.name: Roditis
grapes.note: Pink-skinned white, widely planted, the sole grape of PDO Patra and a component of Anchialos and much retsina.

grapes.name: Savatiano
grapes.note: Greece's most planted white, the backbone of Attica and of retsina; old dry-farmed vines give surprisingly textured, lemony wines.

grapes.name: Limniona
grapes.note: Ancient Thessalian red revived by the Zafeirakis family at Tyrnavos: fresh, peppery and silky.

grapes.name: Mavrodaphne
grapes.note: Dark red of Patras and Kefalonia, famous for fortified sweet wines, increasingly made dry.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains
grapes.note: Moschato Aspro: the grape of Muscat of Samos, Patras, Rio Patras, Kefalonia and Rhodes.

grapes.name: Muscat of Alexandria
grapes.note: Moschato Alexandreias: the grape of Limnos, made dry and sweet.

grapes.name: Robola
grapes.note: Limestone-loving white of Kefalonia, lemony and stony.

grapes.name: Vidiano and Vilana
grapes.note: Crete's whites: Vidiano is the rising star (apricot, herbs, texture), Vilana the traditional base of Peza.

grapes.name: Liatiko, Kotsifali and Mandilaria
grapes.note: Crete's reds: Liatiko (pale, spicy, often sweet) in Dafnes and Sitia; Kotsifali softened by deep-coloured Mandilaria in Peza and Archanes.

grapes.name: Limnio
grapes.note: Probably the Lemnia vine of Aristotle; grown on Limnos and in Halkidiki (Slopes of Meliton).

grapes.name: Debina
grapes.note: High-acid white of Zitsa in Epirus, made still and lightly sparkling.

regions.name: Macedonia
regions.tagline: Xinomavro country: cool mountain slopes, lakes and Greece's most age-worthy reds.
regions.summary: Northern Greece's largest wine region stretches from the lakes of Florina and Amyndeon in the west to Drama and Kavala in the east. Its spine is Xinomavro, the grape behind Naoussa, Amyndeon, Goumenissa and (just over the border in Thessaly) Rapsani, but the region also launched modern Greek white wine at Epanomi and Drama and hosts the historic estate of Domaine Carras on Halkidiki.
regions.history: Macedonian wine was praised in antiquity, and Naoussa was already a merchant town making wine in Ottoman times; Boutari was founded there in 1879. Phylloxera arrived in 1898 and destroyed much of the region before replanting on American rootstock. The 1990s brought a cluster of ambitious estates: Kir-Yianni (Naoussa and Amyndeon), Alpha Estate (Amyndeon), Gerovassiliou and Biblia Chora (Epanomi and Kavala), Pavlidis and Wine Art (Drama), and the Thymiopoulos family's biodynamic work at Trilofo.
regions.terroir: Continental influence and altitude set the tone. Mount Vermio shelters Naoussa; Amyndeon sits at 570 to 750 metres around four lakes that moderate frost; Goumenissa lies on the slopes of Mount Paiko. Soils range from marl and limestone to sand, and sandy pockets in Amyndeon still hold ungrafted vines.
regions.grapes: Xinomavro dominates the reds, with Negoska in Goumenissa; Malagousia, Assyrtiko and Sauvignon Blanc lead whites at Epanomi and Drama; Limnio and international varieties grow on Halkidiki.
regions.styles: Structured dry reds, Blanc de Noirs and rosé sparkling Xinomavro in Amyndeon, aromatic whites, and modern Bordeaux-style blends under PGI Drama and PGI Macedonia.
regions.classification: PDOs: Naoussa, Amyndeon, Goumenissa, Slopes of Meliton. Much of the region's best white wine is PGI (Epanomi, Drama, Macedonia).

regions.name: Thessaly
regions.tagline: Olympus foothills, the Pagasetic Gulf and the revival of Limniona.
regions.summary: Thessaly's plain is cereal country, but its edges grow wine: Rapsani on the lower slopes of Mount Olympus, Anchialos on the Pagasetic Gulf near Volos, Mesenikola beside Lake Plastiras, and the Tyrnavos basin, where the Zafeirakis family rescued Limniona.
regions.history: Rapsani's field blend of Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto was revived by Tsantali from 1991 after decades of neglect. Tyrnavos is also famous for tsipouro, the grape-pomace spirit.
regions.terroir: Olympus gives schist soils and altitude up to around 700 metres; the gulf moderates Anchialos; Mesenikola is inland and higher.
regions.grapes: Xinomavro, Krassato, Stavroto, Limniona, Roditis, Savatiano, Mavro Messenikola, Batiki.

regions.name: Epirus
regions.tagline: Wet, mountainous north-west Greece and the sparkling Debina of Zitsa.
regions.summary: Greece's rainiest mainland region has little vineyard, but Zitsa's Debina is one of the country's classic whites, and the high Metsovo vineyard of Katogi Averoff planted Cabernet Sauvignon at around 1,000 metres in the 1950s.
regions.history: Evangelos Averoff founded Katogi in Metsovo, an early Greek experiment with French grapes at altitude.
regions.terroir: High rainfall, cool nights, clay and limestone around 600 metres at Zitsa.
regions.classification: PDO Zitsa; PGI Epirus and PGI Metsovo.

regions.name: Central Greece and Attica
regions.tagline: Savatiano, Aleppo pine and the home of retsina.
regions.summary: Attica's Mesogeia plain east of Athens was for centuries the heart of retsina, white wine flavoured with Aleppo pine resin. It has no PDO, but old, dry-farmed Savatiano bush vines are being bottled again as serious unresinated wine, and producers such as Papagiannakos, Kechris and Gaia have made modern retsina worth a second look.
regions.history: Resin was used to seal amphorae in antiquity; the flavour stuck. Retsina is protected as a traditional designation. Urban sprawl and the Athens airport have eaten into Mesogeia's vineyards.
regions.terroir: Hot, dry, low rainfall, limestone and red clay.
regions.classification: PGIs (Attiki, Markopoulo and others) and the traditional appellation Retsina.

regions.name: Peloponnese
regions.tagline: Greece's biggest wine region: Nemea's reds, Mantinia's aromatic whites and the sweet wines of Patras.
regions.summary: The Peloponnese makes roughly a quarter of Greek wine and holds seven PDOs. Nemea in the north-east is the largest red appellation in the country; Mantinia on the Arcadian plateau grows Moschofilero at 650 metres; around Patras in the north-west four PDOs cover dry Roditis, fortified Mavrodaphne and two Muscats; and Monemvasia in the far south-east has revived the medieval Malvasia.
regions.history: Nemea links its wine to the ancient Phliasian wine and to Heracles and the Nemean lion. Patras became an export port for currants and Mavrodaphne in the nineteenth century, when Gustav Clauss founded Achaia Clauss (1861). Monemvasia gave its name to Malmsey.
regions.terroir: Mountainous interior, coastal plains, limestone and clay. Altitude bands from 230 to 850 metres in Nemea and the cool Mantinia plateau give real diversity within a warm region.
regions.grapes: Agiorgitiko, Moschofilero, Roditis, Mavrodaphne, Muscat Blanc, Monemvasia, Kydonitsa, Asproudes, Lagorthi, Mavro Kalavritino.
regions.styles: Dry reds, aromatic whites, fortified and sun-dried sweet wines, sparkling Moschofilero.
regions.classification: PDOs: Nemea, Mantinia, Patra, Mavrodaphne of Patras, Muscat of Patras, Muscat of Rio Patras, Monemvasia-Malvasia.

regions.name: Ionian Islands
regions.tagline: Venetian islands and the limestone Robola of Kefalonia.
regions.summary: The Ionian islands were Venetian, never Ottoman, and kept their own wine culture. Kefalonia is the star, with three PDOs: Robola, Muscat of Kefalonia and Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia. Zakynthos keeps the oxidative Verdea tradition.
regions.history: Venetian rule until 1797 linked the islands to Italian markets. The 1953 earthquake destroyed much of Kefalonia.
regions.terroir: Limestone scree on Mount Ainos, where Robola grows on its own roots at 600 to 900 metres in places, gives taut, stony whites.
regions.grapes: Robola, Vostilidi, Tsaousi, Zakynthino, Mavrodaphne, Muscat Blanc.
regions.styles: Mineral dry whites, sweet Muscat and fortified Mavrodaphne.
regions.classification: PDOs: Robola of Kefalonia, Muscat of Kefalonia, Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia.

regions.name: Aegean Islands
regions.tagline: Muscat islands: Samos, Limnos and the ancient amphora ports of Chios and Thasos.
regions.summary: The north-eastern Aegean islands have the deepest classical pedigree in Greek wine (Chios, Thasos, Lesbos) and today two great Muscat traditions: Samos, whose terraces climb past 800 metres, and Limnos, where Muscat of Alexandria is made dry and sweet beside the ancient Limnio grape.
regions.history: Chian and Thasian amphorae carried the luxury wines of the classical world. Samos's Union of Vinicultural Cooperatives, founded in 1934, controls almost all the island's wine.
regions.terroir: Steep schist and limestone terraces on Samos, volcanic soils on Limnos, constant wind.
regions.grapes: Muscat Blanc (Samos), Muscat of Alexandria and Limnio (Limnos), Chidiriotiko on Lesbos.
regions.styles: Vin doux naturel and sun-dried sweet Muscats, dry Muscat, light reds.
regions.classification: PDOs: Samos, Limnos, Muscat of Limnos. PGI Plagies Ampelou covers the slopes of Mount Ampelos on Samos.

regions.name: Cyclades
regions.tagline: Wind, pumice and Assyrtiko: Santorini and Paros.
regions.summary: The Cyclades are dry, windswept and tiny, but Santorini has become the most famous wine island in Greece, and Paros keeps its own two PDOs. Tinos, Naxos and Syros have small new-wave estates on granite and schist.
regions.history: Santorini's sweet Vinsanto was shipped by Venetian and later Russian Orthodox merchants for church use. The Bronze Age town of Akrotiri lies under the island's pumice.
regions.terroir: Volcanic ash and pumice on Santorini; granite on Tinos; marble and schist on Paros. The meltemi forces low training.
regions.grapes: Assyrtiko, Athiri, Aidani, Mavrotragano, Mandilaria, Monemvasia.
regions.styles: Dry, saline whites, Nykteri, Vinsanto, red Paros.

regions.name: Dodecanese
regions.tagline: Rhodes: Athiri on Mount Attavyros and Italian-era sparkling.
regions.summary: Rhodes holds two PDOs, Rhodes and Muscat of Rhodes. Its best vineyards climb the slopes of Mount Attavyros around Embonas, where Athiri gives delicate whites and sparkling wine.
regions.history: Under Italian rule (1912 to 1947) the CAIR company was founded in 1928 and began making sparkling wine.
regions.terroir: Limestone slopes up to about 700 metres under Mount Attavyros.
regions.grapes: Athiri, Mandilaria (Amorgiano), Muscat Blanc, Muscat Trani.
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, light reds, sweet Muscat.

regions.name: Crete
regions.tagline: Minoan wine presses, Vidiano and the Liatiko of Dafnes and Sitia.
regions.summary: Greece's largest island has seven PDOs and a wine history that begins with Minoan presses such as Vathypetro. The centre around Heraklion (Peza, Archanes, Dafnes, Chandakas-Candia and Malvasia Chandakas-Candia) and the east around Sitia (Sitia, Malvasia Sitia) are the main zones. A young generation of producers has made Vidiano, Liatiko and Kotsifali exciting again.
regions.history: Venetian Crete (Candia) exported sweet Malvasia across Europe from the thirteenth to the seventeenth century. The 2011 Malvasia PDOs aim to revive that style.
regions.terroir: Mountains up to 2,456 metres (Psiloritis) shelter northern-facing vineyards from African heat; altitude from 300 to 800 metres; calcareous marl and clay.
regions.grapes: Vidiano, Vilana, Thrapsathiri, Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, Kotsifali, Mandilari, Liatiko, Romeiko.
regions.styles: Textured whites, spicy reds, sweet Liatiko and Malvasia.
regions.classification: PDOs: Peza, Archanes, Dafnes, Sitia, Chandakas-Candia, Malvasia Sitia, Malvasia Chandakas-Candia. PGI Crete covers the island.

gr-amyntaio.name: Amyndeon
gr-amyntaio.summary: The coolest PDO in Greece sits on a high plateau in western Macedonia at 570 to 750 metres, around the lakes Vegoritida, Petron, Zazari and Chimaditida. That altitude and the lakes' moderating effect make Amyndeon the natural home of sparkling and rosé Xinomavro as well as fresher, more aromatic reds than Naoussa's. It is also one of the few PDOs in Greece that allows rosé and sparkling wine.
gr-amyntaio.terroir: Sandy soils in parts of the zone resisted phylloxera, so some ungrafted old Xinomavro survives. Frost and a short season are the risks.
gr-amyntaio.nerd_note: Alpha Estate's ungrafted Xinomavro block 'Hedgehog' sits on sandy soil near the lake.

gr-anchialos.name: Anchialos
gr-anchialos.summary: A small white-wine PDO on the shore of the Pagasetic Gulf near Volos, blending Roditis and Savatiano into fresh, lemony wines for local fish tavernas. Most production is cooperative. The wines are light, crisp and meant for drinking young, with Roditis giving citrus freshness and Savatiano a little more body.
gr-anchialos.terroir: Flat to gently sloping coastal land with sea breezes; light, calcareous soils.

gr-archanes.name: Archanes
gr-archanes.summary: A red-only PDO around Archanes, a Minoan centre where the villa of Vathypetro preserves one of the oldest wine presses in Europe. Kotsifali gives perfume and alcohol, Mandilari colour and grip.
gr-archanes.terroir: Slopes beneath Mount Giouchtas at 300 to 600 metres.
gr-archanes.nerd_note: Vathypetro's Minoan press, a few kilometres south of Archanes, is still visible in situ.

gr-chandakas-candia.name: Chandakas-Candia
gr-chandakas-candia.grapes: Vidiano, Vilana, Assyrtiko, Athiri, Thrapsathiri (white); Kotsifali, Mandilari (red)
gr-chandakas-candia.summary: Created in 2011 around Heraklion (Chandakas was its Byzantine and Arab name, Candia its Venetian one), this PDO gives a home to modern Cretan dry wines, including Vidiano-based whites. White blends lean on Vidiano, Vilana, Thrapsathiri, Assyrtiko and Athiri; reds on Kotsifali and Mandilari.

gr-dafnes.name: Dafnes
gr-dafnes.summary: West of Heraklion, Dafnes is the home of Liatiko, an early-ripening Cretan red that gives pale, spicy dry wines and, traditionally, sweet wines from sun-dried grapes. Douloufakis is the leading estate.
gr-dafnes.terroir: Hills of 300 to 600 metres, calcareous clay.

gr-goumenissa.name: Goumenissa
gr-goumenissa.summary: On the lower slopes of Mount Paiko north-west of Thessaloniki, Goumenissa blends Xinomavro with the softer, deeply coloured Negoska. The result is rounder and earlier-drinking than Naoussa but keeps Xinomavro's spice and acidity. Small family estates dominate.
gr-goumenissa.terroir: Paiko's foothills at 200 to 400 metres, sandy clay and limestone, a more open, slightly warmer position than Naoussa.
gr-goumenissa.nerd_note: Negoska is grown almost nowhere else; its name probably comes from the old Slavic name of Naoussa.

gr-limnos.name: Limnos
gr-limnos.summary: Limnos makes dry, floral white wine from Muscat of Alexandria, unusual in Greece, and reds from Limnio, a grape probably identical to the Lemnia vine that Aristotle described. Volcanic soils and constant wind keep yields low.
gr-limnos.terroir: Volcanic and clay soils on a flat, windy island in the north Aegean.

gr-malvasia-chandakas-candia.name: Malvasia Chandakas-Candia
gr-malvasia-chandakas-candia.grapes: Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, Vidiano, Muscat Blanc, Liatiko, Thrapsathiri, Assyrtiko, Athiri
gr-malvasia-chandakas-candia.summary: The Heraklion version of the Malvasia revival: sweet wines from sun-dried grapes, reviving the style Venetian Candia exported across Europe. Malvasia di Candia Aromatica leads the blend with Vidiano, Muscat Blanc, Liatiko, Thrapsathiri, Assyrtiko and Athiri permitted. Production is small; Heraklion-area producers are still building the style.

gr-malvasia-paros.name: Malvasia Paros
gr-malvasia-paros.summary: One of the four Malvasia PDOs created in 2011: sweet wine from sun-dried Monemvasia grapes, aged in oak. Production is tiny. Its rules allow Monemvasia with a little Assyrtiko. Like the other three Malvasia PDOs of 2011, it aims to revive the sweet wine style Venetian merchants once traded from the Aegean.

gr-malvasia-sitias.name: Malvasia Sitia
gr-malvasia-sitias.grapes: Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, Muscat Blanc, Liatiko, Thrapsathiri, Assyrtiko, Athiri
gr-malvasia-sitias.summary: A 2011 PDO for sweet wines in the medieval Cretan Malvasia tradition, made from sun-dried grapes around Sitia. Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, Muscat Blanc, Liatiko, Thrapsathiri, Assyrtiko and Athiri are permitted. Production is still tiny, but it gives eastern Crete a sweet-wine identity alongside dry Sitia.

gr-mantinia.name: Mantinia
gr-mantinia.summary: On a high plateau around Tripoli in Arcadia, at roughly 650 metres, Mantinia makes the most aromatic dry white in Greece from pink-skinned Moschofilero: rose petal, citrus blossom and spice, with crisp acidity and moderate alcohol. Sparkling Mantinia is permitted, and the cool, late harvest (often into October) makes this one of the latest-picked PDOs in Greece.
gr-mantinia.terroir: Cold winters, frost risk and a short season on the plateau of ancient Mantineia; clay and limestone soils.
gr-mantinia.nerd_note: Moschofilero is a 'grey' grape: skin colour ranges from pale pink to purple, and longer skin contact gives copper-tinted whites and rosés.

gr-mavrodafni-kefallinias.name: Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia
gr-mavrodafni-kefallinias.summary: Kefalonia's fortified red, made in the same style as Mavrodaphne of Patras. Mavrodaphne may in fact originate in the Ionian islands, and Kefalonian producers also make it dry. EU rules allow Korinthiaki (Black Corinth) alongside Mavrodaphne, as in Patras.

gr-mavrodafni-patron.name: Mavrodaphne of Patras
gr-mavrodafni-patron.summary: A fortified red made since the nineteenth century around Patras, sweet and raisiny with notes of coffee, caramel and dried fig, often aged oxidatively for years in barrels. Achaia Clauss made it famous; Parparoussis and Antonopoulos have revived higher-quality versions, including old solera-style bottlings.
gr-mavrodafni-patron.nerd_note: Local lore says Gustav Clauss named the wine after his late fiancée Daphne; the grape name 'black laurel' is older than that story.

gr-mesenikola.name: Mesenikola
gr-mesenikola.grapes: Mavro Messenikola with Carignan and Syrah
gr-mesenikola.summary: Named after a village near Lake Plastiras in the foothills of the Agrafa mountains, this PDO is built around the rare local Mavro Messenikola, softened with Carignan and Syrah. The wines are light, peppery reds; very little leaves the region.
gr-mesenikola.terroir: Hillside vineyards above the Thessalian plain at around 200 to 500 metres.

gr-monemvasia-malvasia.name: Monemvasia-Malvasia
gr-monemvasia-malvasia.summary: Registered in 2011 to revive the legendary Malmsey of the Middle Ages, this PDO covers sweet wines from sun-dried grapes made in Laconia around the rock of Monemvasia. The rules require long barrel ageing, and the best wines are amber, honeyed and nutty. Monemvasia Winery (Tsimbidis) led the revival.
gr-monemvasia-malvasia.terroir: Hills of south-eastern Laconia with limestone soils, hot and dry.
gr-monemvasia-malvasia.nerd_note: The grape called Monemvasia and the Italian Malvasia family share a name and a trade route, but DNA shows Monemvasia is a distinct Greek variety.

gr-moschato-patron.name: Muscat of Patras
gr-moschato-patron.summary: Sweet Muscat from the hills around Patras, either fortified or made from sun-dried grapes; fragrant with orange blossom and apricot. The grape is the small-berried Muscat Blanc (Moschato Aspro), the same as on Samos, grown on the hills behind the city alongside the vineyards of PDO Patra and Mavrodaphne of Patras.
gr-moschato-patron.terroir: Slopes of Achaia with calcareous soils.

gr-moschatos-kefallinias.name: Muscat of Kefalonia
gr-moschatos-kefallinias.summary: Sweet Muscat from Kefalonia, fortified or from sun-dried grapes; small production, mostly sold on the island. The grape is Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, grown on the same dry limestone as Robola. Like Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia, it is a small production sold mostly on the island.

gr-moschatos-limnou.name: Muscat of Limnos
gr-moschatos-limnou.summary: The sweet partner to PDO Limnos, fortified or from sun-dried grapes; grapey and floral. Unlike the Muscat Blanc of Samos and Patras, it is made from Muscat of Alexandria (Moschato Alexandreias), fortified or from sun-dried grapes, on the island's volcanic soils.

gr-moschatos-riou-patras.name: Muscat of Rio Patras
gr-moschatos-riou-patras.summary: A smaller Muscat appellation centred on Rio, east of Patras at the narrows of the Gulf of Corinth, for fortified or sun-dried sweet Muscat. Parparoussis makes the reference examples.

gr-moschatos-rodou.name: Muscat of Rhodes
gr-moschatos-rodou.grapes: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Muscat Trani
gr-moschatos-rodou.summary: Sweet Muscat from Rhodes, light and floral; a small appellation, mostly cooperative. The vineyards share the slopes of the island with PDO Rhodes, and the wine is usually lighter and more floral than the Muscats of Samos or Patras. Production is small.

gr-naoussa.name: Naoussa
gr-naoussa.summary:
Naoussa is the home of Xinomavro and Greece's most serious red wine appellation. The town sits on the eastern flank of Mount Vermio, and its vineyards run along the slopes at roughly 150 to 450 metres, with Kir-Yianni, Thymiopoulos, Dalamara, Karydas, Chrisohoou and the founding house of Boutari (1879) at the core of the local tradition. The wine must be pure Xinomavro, a grape whose name means 'acid-black' though it is rarely black: in the glass Naoussa is translucent garnet, with high acidity, firm tannins and a perfume of sour cherry, tomato leaf, olive, dried rose and spice that develops towards leather and forest floor over ten to twenty years.

The comparison with Barolo is inevitable and partly fair. Like Nebbiolo, Xinomavro is sensitive to site and vintage, slow to reveal itself and unforgiving of over-extraction. The modern debate in Naoussa mirrors Piedmont's: large old casks versus new oak, early drinking versus long ageing, single-vineyard bottlings versus blends of villages. Growers increasingly name their sites, from Trilofo and Fytia in the south to Gastra, Yianakochori and Ramnista.
gr-naoussa.terroir: Mount Vermio shelters the vineyards from cold north-westerly winds and drains cool air down the slopes at night. Soils vary from marl and clay to limestone and sandy loam; sandier sites give lighter, more perfumed wines, clay sites darker, firmer ones. The continental climate gives cold winters and warm summers with a long autumn.
gr-naoussa.nerd_note: Kir-Yianni was founded in 1997 by Yiannis Boutaris, who left his family firm to make site-driven Xinomavro; he later became mayor of Thessaloniki.

gr-nemea.name: Nemea
gr-nemea.summary:
Nemea is Greece's largest red wine appellation and the home of Agiorgitiko (St George's grape). It covers 17 villages in the hills of Korinthia, plus two (Gymno and Malandreni) in north-western Argolida, making it the only Greek PDO spread across two prefectures. Agiorgitiko is the Merlot of Greece in its generosity: soft tannins, plum, cherry and sweet spice, but with enough freshness at altitude to age well. Styles range from fresh, fruity reds to oak-aged reserves and rarer semi-sweet, fortified and sun-dried sweet wines; rosé and blends are made but must be labelled as PGI.

The appellation links itself to the ancient Phliasian wine and to the myth of Heracles and the Nemean lion; locals still call the wine 'blood of Hercules'. The Temple of Zeus at Ancient Nemea stands among the vines.
gr-nemea.terroir: Vineyards climb from about 230 metres on the valley floor to around 850 metres. Producers talk of three altitude bands: a low zone (Nemea, Ancient Nemea, Ancient Kleones, Leontio, Gymno) of richer red clay; a middle zone (Koutsi, Dafni) widely considered the sweet spot for structured reds; and a high zone (Asprokampos, Psari, Kastraki, Kefalari and others) of cooler, stonier sites that give fresher wines. These sub-zones are informal and not codified in the PDO rules; proposals to formalise them have been discussed for years.
gr-nemea.nerd_note: Koutsi has the reputation of a grand cru, and wines from it often carry the village name in fantasy brand names even though the PDO does not allow sub-zone labelling.

gr-paros.name: Paros
gr-paros.grapes: Mandilaria with the white Monemvasia (red); Monemvasia (white)
gr-paros.summary: Paros has one of the oddest rules in Europe: its red must blend the dark Mandilaria with the white Monemvasia, a historic practice that softens Mandilaria's tannin and colour. Moraitis is the main producer. Old bush vines on sand and schist are often ungrafted.
gr-paros.terroir: Sandy, granite and schist soils, strong winds.

gr-patra.name: Patra
gr-patra.summary: The dry white appellation of Patras, made only from Roditis grown on the slopes of the Achaean mountains. Higher vineyards give citrus, minerally wines; many producers bottle Roditis as PGI instead.
gr-patra.terroir: Slopes from about 250 to 800 metres facing the Gulf of Patras.

gr-peza.name: Peza
gr-peza.summary: South of Heraklion around the village of Peza, Crete's largest PDO makes fresh whites from Vilana and reds from Kotsifali blended with Mandilari for colour and tannin. The Peza Union of cooperatives remains important, alongside family estates such as Lyrarakis and Stilianou.
gr-peza.terroir: Hillsides at roughly 300 to 600 metres under the Lasithi and Psiloritis ranges; calcareous clay.

gr-plagies-melitona.name: Slopes of Meliton
gr-plagies-melitona.grapes: Red: Limnio with Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc; white: Athiri, Roditis, Assyrtiko
gr-plagies-melitona.summary: A one-estate appellation on the Sithonia peninsula of Halkidiki, created for Domaine Porto Carras, which John Carras planted from the 1960s with advice from Émile Peynaud. Its red blend of Limnio and Cabernet was the first Greek appellation to include international varieties, and the estate trained a generation of Greek winemakers, including Evangelos Gerovassiliou.
gr-plagies-melitona.terroir: Granite and schist slopes above the sea on Mount Meliton (Itamos).
gr-plagies-melitona.nerd_note: Malagousia's rescue began here: Professor Vassilis Logothetis collected the near-extinct vine and Gerovassiliou propagated it at Porto Carras before planting it at Epanomi.

gr-rapsani.name: Rapsani
gr-rapsani.summary: Rapsani is the Mount Olympus appellation, a historic field blend of Xinomavro with two local grapes, Krassato and Stavroto, grown on the mountain's south-eastern slopes above the Tempi valley. Tsantali revived it from 1991 and still dominates; the wines are spicy, medium-bodied and grow more refined as the vineyards climb.
gr-rapsani.terroir: Schist soils between about 300 and 700 metres on Olympus, with the Aegean a few kilometres east. Producers distinguish lower, middle and upper zones.
gr-rapsani.nerd_note: Tsantali's Rapsani Grande Reserve comes from the highest, schist-rich parcels, which locals call the 'old vines of the gods'.

gr-robola-kefallinias.name: Robola of Kefalonia
gr-robola-kefallinias.summary: Kefalonia's flagship white grows on the limestone flanks of Mount Ainos, often around the Omala valley, giving lean, lemony, stony wines with a smoky edge. Many vines are ungrafted because phylloxera could not spread in the loose limestone scree. The Robola cooperative (Orealios Gaia) handles much of the crop.
gr-robola-kefallinias.terroir: Limestone scree at up to around 900 metres, very poor soils, strong sun and sea winds.
gr-robola-kefallinias.nerd_note: Robola was long assumed to be Italy's Ribolla Gialla; DNA analysis says the two are unrelated.

gr-rodos.name: Rhodes
gr-rodos.summary: Rhodes' PDO covers delicate whites and sparkling wine from Athiri grown on the slopes of Mount Attavyros around Embonas, and reds from Mandilaria (locally Amorgiano). CAIR, founded under Italian rule in 1928, has made sparkling wine here for nearly a century.
gr-rodos.terroir: Limestone slopes up to about 700 metres on the island's highest mountain.

gr-samos.name: Samos
gr-samos.summary:
Muscat of Samos has been one of Greece's most exported wines for over a century, and it is a model of cooperative winemaking: the Union of Vinicultural Cooperatives of Samos, founded in 1934, buys grapes from thousands of growers who tend small terraces on the island's mountains. The range runs from fortified vin doux (Samos Doux, Grand Cru) to Nectar, made from sun-dried grapes and aged in oak, and long-aged Anthemis and Samos Vin Doux Naturel Grand Cru bottlings.

Altitude matters: terraces climb from near sea level to over 800 metres on Mount Ampelos and Mount Kerkis, and the higher sites ripen weeks later, giving finer, more aromatic Muscat. The same mountains are covered by PGI Plagies Ampelou, used for dry wines.
gr-samos.terroir: Steep, hand-built stone terraces of schist and limestone; the north-facing slopes are cooler and wetter.
producers: Union of Vinicultural Cooperatives of Samos (EOSS)
gr-samos.nerd_note: Samos was a tax-free supplier of Muscat to the Vatican and the Catholic church for sacramental wine in the twentieth century.

gr-santorini.name: Santorini
gr-santorini.grapes: Assyrtiko (at least 75% for dry white), Athiri, Aidani; Vinsanto mostly Assyrtiko with Aidani
gr-santorini.summary:
Santorini makes the most distinctive white wine in Greece and one of the most distinctive anywhere. The island is the rim of a collapsed volcano: the Bronze Age eruption that buried Akrotiri left a blanket of ash and pumice with almost no organic matter and no clay, and on it grows Assyrtiko, a grape that keeps searing acidity under a hot sun. Dry Santorini (at least 75% Assyrtiko, the rest Athiri and Aidani) tastes of lemon, flint and sea spray, gains weight and smoky complexity with age, and is the reason Assyrtiko is now planted from Macedonia to South Australia.

Two traditional styles carry the island's history. Nykteri, from 'night work', was originally picked and pressed at night to avoid the heat; today it is a richer, oak-aged dry white. Vinsanto, the island's sweet wine (the name probably means 'wine of Santorini', not 'holy wine'), is made from grapes dried in the sun for around two weeks and aged at least two years in oak, giving a dark, figgy, acid-lit dessert wine that can outlive its makers.

Scarcity is part of the story. The island has about 1,200 hectares of vines, shrinking under hotels and villas, and yields are tiny: drought, wind and old vines often give a fraction of the legal limit, and the 2023 and 2024 crops were painfully small. Prices for top bottlings have risen sharply.
gr-santorini.terroir: No clay means no phylloxera, so vines grow on their own roots, some root systems claimed to be centuries old; growers periodically cut the old trunk away and let a new shoot grow from the same roots. The vines are trained low as kouloures, baskets woven from the canes, with the grapes hanging inside, out of the wind and sun. Night humidity from the sea is absorbed by the porous pumice and keeps unirrigated vines alive through summers with almost no rain. Sub-zones such as Pyrgos, Megalochori, Akrotiri, Oia and Imerovigli give perceptibly different wines, and producers now bottle them separately.
gr-santorini.nerd_note: The basket vines are rewoven every winter and can be 'rejuvenated' by cutting back to the root, so a vine's above-ground part may be young while its roots are hundreds of years old.

gr-sitia.name: Sitia
gr-sitia.grapes: Liatiko and Mandilari (red); Vilana and Thrapsathiri (white)
gr-sitia.summary: Eastern Crete's PDO, with some of the island's highest vineyards (up to around 600 metres or more), makes Liatiko reds, white blends and sweet Liatiko. Economou's long-aged Liatiko from the Ziros plateau is a cult bottle.
gr-sitia.terroir: Dry, windy eastern Crete; terraces and plateaus above Sitia.

gr-zitsa.name: Zitsa
gr-zitsa.summary: In the mountains north of Ioannina, Zitsa makes still and lightly sparkling white wine from Debina, a high-acid grape with apple and white-flower aromas. The semi-sparkling style is traditional, and the region was praised by Byron, who stayed at the monastery of Profitis Ilias in 1809.
gr-zitsa.terroir: Around 600 metres, high rainfall, cool nights, clay-limestone soils. Grapes ripen late and keep low alcohol.
gr-zitsa.nerd_note: Debina is one of very few Greek grapes routinely made as a pétillant wine in a traditional regional style.

sites.name: Akrotiri (Bronze Age Thera)
sites.text: The Minoan-era town buried by the eruption of Thera around 1600 BC, preserved with storage jars, pithoi and drinking vessels under metres of pumice. The same eruption laid down the ash in which Santorini's ungrafted Assyrtiko now grows, which makes this the rare archaeological site where the ancient catastrophe is also the modern terroir.

sites.name: Vathypetro Minoan wine press
sites.text: A Minoan villa south of Archanes, built around 1600 BC, with a stone wine press, a spouted basin and storage jars still in place. It is one of the oldest wine-making installations in Europe and sits inside today's PDO Archanes.

sites.name: Dikili Tash
sites.text: A Neolithic tell near Philippi in eastern Macedonia where charred grape pips and pressed grape skins from around 4300 BC point to early wine making, perhaps the oldest such evidence in the Aegean.

sites.name: Palace of Nestor, Pylos
sites.text: Mycenaean palace of the thirteenth century BC whose Linear B archive records wine and vineyards and whose wine magazine held dozens of storage jars, some sealed with clay stamped with the wine ideogram.

sites.name: Ancient Thasos (Limenas)
sites.text: The harbour city of Thasos, whose fifth-century BC inscriptions regulated the sale of wine and whose stamped amphorae spread its famous sweet wine across the Aegean and Black Sea.

sites.name: Ariousian hills of Chios
sites.text: The north-west of Chios, around Volissos, produced Ariousian wine, the most prized wine of classical Greece, shipped in amphorae stamped with a sphinx. Vines barely survive there today.

sites.name: Temple of Zeus, Ancient Nemea
sites.text: The fourth-century BC temple of the Nemean Games stands among Agiorgitiko vineyards; the site museum displays wine vessels and the stadium sits a short walk away.

sites.name: Monemvasia
sites.text: The fortified rock-town whose port gave its name to Malvasia and Malmsey, the sweet wine Venetian galleys carried to Europe. PDO Monemvasia-Malvasia (2011) revives the style in the hills inland.

sites.name: Domaine Sigalas
sites.text: Paris Sigalas, a mathematician, founded his winery in 1991 on the flat Baxedes plain below Oia, in Santorini's north. Its Assyrtikos, single-site Kavalieros, Nykteri and Vinsanto are among the island's references, and the estate has bottled rare Mavrotragano reds.

sites.name: Hatzidakis Winery
sites.text: Founded by Haridimos Hatzidakis in 1997 near Pyrgos and run by his family since his death in 2017, Hatzidakis makes some of Santorini's most intense, low-intervention Assyrtikos from old vines, including the single-site Mylos and Skitali bottlings.

sites.name: Gaia Wines Santorini
sites.text: Gaia's island winery occupies an old tomato-processing plant on the beach near Exo Gonia; Thalassitis ('from the sea') was one of the first Santorini wines to win international attention, and the winery experiments with ageing wine under the sea.

sites.name: Estate Argyros
sites.text: A family estate at Episkopi Gonias founded in 1903, with some of the largest holdings of old Assyrtiko on the island and a library of Vinsanto aged for decades.

sites.name: Santo Wines
sites.text: The Union of Santorini Cooperatives, founded in 1947, with a cliff-top winery near Pyrgos above the caldera. It processes much of the island's crop.

sites.name: Kir-Yianni
sites.text: Yiannis Boutaris founded Kir-Yianni in 1997 on the family's Yiannakochori vineyard east of Naoussa, aiming for site-specific Xinomavro (Ramnista, Diaporos) and later adding the Samaropetra estate in Amyndeon.

sites.name: Thymiopoulos Vineyards
sites.text: Apostolos Thymiopoulos farms biodynamically at Trilofo and Fytia in the southern part of Naoussa, making perfumed, transparent Xinomavro such as 'Earth and Sky' and the single-vineyard Ramnista.

sites.name: Boutari Naoussa winery
sites.text: Boutari was founded in Naoussa in 1879 and its Naoussa red was for decades the bottle that defined Xinomavro abroad; its Naoussa winery is at Stenimachos, east of the town.

sites.name: Ktima Gerovassiliou
sites.text: Evangelos Gerovassiliou's estate at Epanomi, south of Thessaloniki, planted from 1981 on sandy soils by the sea. It made Malagousia famous and houses a museum of corkscrews and wine tools.

sites.name: Domaine Porto Carras
sites.text: The estate John Carras built on the slopes of Mount Meliton from the 1960s with Émile Peynaud's advice, one of the first modern wineries in Greece and the sole producer of PDO Slopes of Meliton.

sites.name: Alpha Estate
sites.text: Founded in 1997 by Angelos Iatridis and Makis Mavridis on the Amyndeon plateau, Alpha is known for its ungrafted 'Hedgehog' Xinomavro and its Malagousia and Syrah blends.

sites.name: Domaine Skouras
sites.text: George Skouras, trained in Dijon, built his winery at Malandreni near Argos; Megas Oenos (Agiorgitiko and Cabernet) was a landmark Greek blend, and his Nemea wines come from high vineyards around Gymno.

sites.name: Gaia Estate Nemea
sites.text: Gaia's Nemea winery at Koutsi, in the middle altitude band many consider Nemea's best, makes Gaia Estate Agiorgitiko, one of the benchmarks for ageable Nemea.

sites.name: Domaine Tselepos
sites.text: Yiannis Tselepos, trained in Burgundy, founded his winery at Rizes near Tegea on the Mantinia plateau in 1989; his Moschofilero, sparkling Amalia and Avlotopi Cabernet are classics.

sites.name: Achaia Clauss
sites.text: The castle-like winery Gustav Clauss founded in 1861 in the hills above Patras, home of the most famous Mavrodaphne and of cellars holding barrels and bottles back to the nineteenth century.

sites.name: Samos Wine Museum (EOSS)
sites.text: The cooperative union's old winery at Malagari near Vathy has been turned into a museum of Samian Muscat, with giant barrels and old presses; the working winery is at Karlovasi.
producers: Union of Vinicultural Cooperatives of Samos

sites.name: Orealios Gaia Robola Cooperative
sites.text: The Robola producers' cooperative in the Omala valley on Kefalonia, beneath the limestone flanks of Mount Ainos, produces a large share of PDO Robola.

sites.name: Monemvasia Winery (Tsimbidis)
sites.text: George Tsimbidis led the revival of Monemvasia-Malvasia, the first modern sweet wine in the medieval style, from vineyards at Velies in Laconia.

sites.name: Emery Winery
sites.text: Founded in 1923 at Embonas beneath Mount Attavyros, Emery makes Athiri whites and sparkling wines from some of the highest vineyards on Rhodes.

sites.name: Lyrarakis Winery
sites.text: The Lyrarakis family at Alagni, south of Heraklion, rescued the Cretan whites Dafni and Plyto from near extinction in the 1990s and is one of the leading names in Peza and Archanes.

sites.name: Douloufakis Winery
sites.text: A family winery in the village of Dafnes, west of Heraklion, run by Nikos Douloufakis, making benchmark Liatiko in dry and sun-dried sweet styles alongside Vidiano. Dafnes is the PDO built around Liatiko, an early-ripening Cretan red that gives pale, spicy, surprisingly fresh wines.

sites.name: Economou Winery, Ziros
sites.text: Yiannis Economou, who trained in Piedmont and Bordeaux, makes long-aged Liatiko from the Ziros plateau in eastern Crete, released after many years in cellar.

sites.name: Tsantali Rapsani
sites.text: Tsantali revived the Rapsani appellation from 1991, terracing the Olympus foothills and restoring the Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto field blend.

sites.name: Zafeirakis Winery
sites.text: The Zafeirakis family at Tyrnavos in Thessaly revived Limniona, a nearly lost ancient red, and made it a symbol of Greek variety rediscovery.

sites.name: Glinavos Winery, Zitsa
sites.text: A family winery in Zitsa, in the mountains north of Ioannina, and the reference producer for the PDO's still and semi-sparkling Debina. The high, wet Epirus climate keeps the grapes late-ripening and fresh, with low alcohol.

sites.name: Mesogeia retsina vineyards
sites.text: The plain east of Athens around Spata, Markopoulo and Koropi, historic home of Savatiano bush vines and retsina, now squeezed by suburbs and the airport.
